![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/a3623402e5d5df9339f1a3bb615c92ff5fcff9ae8d96c3630c5cb847a3038eda.png)

Water is leaking out of a cone-shaped container so that the volume of the water decreases at a rate of $12\,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/min}.$ The height of the container is three times its base radius. Find the rate of decrease of the radius of the water's surface when the radius is $6\,\text{in}.$ Do not round the answer.

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The radius is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} $\text{in}/\text{min}.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the conical volume of water and $r$ be the radius of its surface. Both of these quantities, as well as the water's volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-12\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=6\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we want the rate of change, which is $r.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$

We're told that the height is always three times its base radius. So, we have $h=3r.$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}(3r) \\  & =\pi {r}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =3\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-12 & =3\pi (6)^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ -12 & =108\pi \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{9\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the water's surface decreases at a rate of $\frac{1}{9\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{min}.$
